title: Foreign Body Removal
keywords: button battery in the nose or ear is a true emergency, tissue necrosis starts within hours
button battery in the esophagus is also emergent, remove within 2 hours if possible
a stomach button battery in an asymptomatic child over 5 or with a battery under 20mm can often be observed
irrigation is first-line for many ear/nose foreign bodies before instrumentation
plain radiography misses organic and most glass-thin material, ultrasound or CT if suspicion remains high after a negative X-ray
sources: National Battery Ingestion Hotline / Poison Control button-battery management guidance.
Davies PH, Benger JR. Foreign bodies in the nose and ear: a review of techniques for removal in the emergency department. J Accid Emerg Med. 2000.

changelog.change: Initial entry — a genuine content gap (Content audit 2026-09-14, Batch 5) — zero existing coverage of any foreign-body removal topic. Button battery content given the most detailed treatment given the genuine time-sensitivity and severity if missed.
Reformatted for reading on a phone: long paragraphs broken into short paragraphs and lists. Wording and clinical content unchanged.

purpose: Common ED foreign body scenarios (ear, nose, soft tissue, cornea) and their removal techniques — and the one true emergency in this category: button battery ingestion or insertion, which needs to be recognized and acted on fast.
entryPrompt: Button battery in the nose, ear, or esophagus is a genuine time-critical emergency — screen for it first before working through routine foreign-body technique.

nodes.prompt: Button battery — screen for this FIRST, it changes everything
nodes.body:
ESOPHAGUS: a button battery lodged in the ESOPHAGUS causes serious tissue burns that can occur within as little as 2 HOURS — this is a true emergency: remove it immediately (endoscopy), do not defer to routine ENT/GI scheduling.
- Larger (≥ 20mm) and lithium batteries are the most dangerous and are more likely to lodge in the esophagus in the first place, especially in children under 6.

NOSE OR EAR: a NASAL or AURAL button battery is also emergent for the same reason (local tissue necrosis, septal perforation or tympanic membrane/ossicular damage can occur fast) — remove urgently, don't treat it as a routine foreign body.

STOMACH: a button battery that has already passed into the STOMACH is different — most pass on their own and can be managed with observation, with the specific approach depending on the patient's age and the battery's size.
- Call the National Battery Ingestion Hotline (1-800-498-8666, staffed 24 hours) for current specific guidance rather than relying on a fixed rule here, since this guidance is actively maintained.

HONEY OR SUCRALFATE: if the child can swallow, honey or sucralfate suspension (10 mL every 10 minutes, up to 6 doses) may slow esophageal injury while arranging removal — this is an adjunct that buys time, NOT a substitute for emergent removal of a battery still lodged in the esophagus.

For most solid objects (beads, small toys):
- Irrigation with warm water is a reasonable first attempt for many objects — if the object isn't organic/vegetable matter (which can swell with water and become harder to remove), and if the tympanic membrane is confirmed intact.
- Alligator forceps or a right-angle hook/curette under direct visualization for a graspable object.

LIVE INSECT: kill it first (mineral oil or lidocaine instilled into the canal) before attempting removal — a struggling insect causes significant pain and can burrow deeper.

Avoid multiple blind instrumentation attempts that push the object further in — if an initial reasonable attempt fails, ENT referral is appropriate rather than repeated attempts risking canal trauma or tympanic membrane injury.

Position the child sitting up, good lighting, a nasal speculum for visualization.

Screen for button battery FIRST (see above) — do not treat a nasal battery as a routine foreign body.

Techniques:
- Direct instrument removal (forceps/hook) for a visible, graspable object.
- The 'parent's kiss' technique: parent occludes the unaffected nostril and gives a short sharp puff of breath into the child's mouth while the child's mouth is sealed around the parent's, generating positive pressure that can expel the object. Works well for a round/smooth object and avoids instrumentation entirely — often a good first attempt in a cooperative-enough child.
- Positive-pressure techniques (bag-valve-mask over the mouth with the unaffected nostril occluded) are an alternative when the parent's-kiss technique isn't feasible.

History and mechanism guide suspicion (glass, wood, metal fragments from a laceration or puncture).

IMAGING: plain radiography readily detects metal and glass (even small glass fragments are usually radiopaque, contrary to old teaching) but MISSES organic material (wood, plastic, vegetable matter) reliably. If suspicion remains high after a negative X-ray, especially with a history suggesting organic material, get an ultrasound or CT rather than assuming a negative X-ray excludes a retained foreign body.

EXPLORATION: local exploration under adequate anesthesia and good lighting/hemostasis (a bloodless field, using a tourniquet on a digit if appropriate) for a foreign body accessible without extensive dissection.

Refer for a deep, small, or difficult-to-localize object rather than extensive blind ED exploration that risks more tissue damage than the foreign body itself.

Fluorescein exam under a Wood's lamp/slit lamp to localize.

Screen carefully for an associated open globe injury (mechanism suggesting high-velocity/metal-on-metal — think grinding, hammering) BEFORE attempting removal — an open globe changes management entirely (shield the eye, do not manipulate further, emergent ophthalmology).

A superficial foreign body can often be removed with a moistened cotton-tip applicator or, if that fails, an eye spud/needle under slit-lamp magnification by an experienced provider.

A rust ring from a metallic foreign body may need a separate removal step (burr) — can often be deferred to ophthalmology follow-up rather than aggressively pursued in the ED if removal isn't straightforward.

checklist: Button battery screened for and treated with emergent urgency if in the nose, ear, or esophagus — NOT managed as a routine foreign body
Open globe injury excluded before attempting removal of any corneal/ocular foreign body
Live insect killed before ear-canal removal attempted
Repeated blind instrumentation avoided — escalate to specialist referral after a reasonable initial attempt fails, rather than risking further tissue trauma
Organic soft-tissue foreign bodies actively considered even after a negative plain X-ray, given plain film's known blind spot for that material
